claims.claim: In standard English, a singular subject takes a singular verb form and a plural subject takes a plural verb form; in the present simple, the -s ending marks the third-person singular verb.
The verb be has distinct present-tense forms for person and number (I am, you are, he/she/it is, we/they are) and past forms was and were, so agreement with be is clearly visible.
Compound subjects joined by and take a plural verb, except when the parts name a single idea or unit, which takes a singular verb.
When a compound subject is joined by or or nor, the verb agrees with the part of the subject nearest the verb.
Most indefinite pronouns (everyone, everybody, anybody, someone, each, either, neither, nobody, no one, nothing, and others) take a singular verb because they treat the group as a single unit.

Collective nouns such as team, family, committee, class, and group are generally treated as singular and take a singular verb; some varieties of English allow a plural verb when the members act separately.
In sentences beginning with there is or there are (and here), the subject follows the verb, and the verb agrees with the noun that follows it.
A number of takes a plural verb because it means "several," while the number of takes a singular verb because it names a single count.
Words and phrases between the subject and the verb, including prepositional phrases and expressions such as with, together with, including, and as well as, do not change the number of the subject.

Some English dialects omit the -s on singular verbs or use a singular verb with a plural subject; standard written English follows the agreement pattern, and the lesson describes the variation without judging speakers.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether collective nouns take a singular or a plural verb
positions: North American practice treats team, family, and committee as singular, as in "The team runs during practice" (Purdue OWL).
Some varieties of English, especially British English, allow a plural verb when the members act separately, as in "The audience were silent" (Cambridge Dictionary Grammar).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Teach the singular general rule as the standard for North American academic writing and present the plural option as a recognized variation tied to meaning and variety.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether indefinite pronouns like all, some, none, and any are singular or plural
positions: Most indefinite pronouns are always singular (Purdue OWL; OpenStax).
A small group, including all, any, none, some, and many, can take a singular or plural verb depending on the noun they refer to (Writing for Success).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Present the always-singular group as the main rule and note the small varying group as a follow-up detail.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether English requires the -s on third-person singular verbs
positions: Standard written English requires it, as in "The bus leaves in five minutes" (OpenStax).
Some English dialects omit the -s on singular verbs or use a singular verb with a plural subject (OpenStax dialect note).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Teach the standard pattern for academic and professional writing and describe the variation neutrally, matching the subject's no-deficit framing.

sourceRecords.title: Subject-Verb Agreement
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A per the subject source map. Read live via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200). Supports the basic singular/plural rule, compound subjects with and and with or/nor including the nearer-subject rule, don't/doesn't with singular and plural subjects, the singular indefinite pronouns (each, each one, either, neither, everyone, everybody, anybody, anyone, nobody, somebody, someone, no one), collective nouns as singular (group, team, committee, class, family), there is/there are with the subject following the verb, amounts as single units (five dollars is), and expressions that do not change the subject's number (with, together with, including, accompanied by, in addition to, as well as). All rights reserved; reference only; all lesson examples are original.

sourceRecords.title: 6.6 Editing Focus: Subject-Verb Agreement, Writing Guide with Handbook
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A per the subject source map. Read live via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200). Supports the singular-subject/singular-verb and plural-subject/plural-verb rule, compound subjects with and (with the single-idea exception: "Red beans and rice is my favorite meal"), the or/nor nearest-word rule, indefinite pronouns (most take a singular verb; the singular list is given), agreement when the verb comes before the subject including there constructions, intervening words between subject and verb, and the dialect note that some English dialects omit the -s or use a singular verb with a plural subject (framed neutrally in the lesson).

sourceRecords.title: 2.2 Subject-Verb Agreement, Writing for Success
sourceRecords.provider: Writing for Success (Saylor Academy open-textbook mirror)
sourceRecords.notes: Verified OER. Read live via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200). Supports agreement as a match in number and person, the present-tense forms of be, have, and do (I am / you are / he, she, it is / they are), the -s on third-person singular verbs, the always-singular indefinite pronouns with the single-unit rationale for everybody, the small group of indefinite pronouns that can take either verb form (all, any, none, some, many), collective nouns as an error source, and here/there constructions with the subject after the verb.

sourceRecords.title: Subject-verb agreement (English Grammar Today)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B substitute for the source map's British Council entry (British Council LearnEnglish is curl-hostile and pages are retired; see subject research notes). Read live via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200). Supports the person-and-number matching definition of agreement (concord), the third-person singular -s ("He hates being in hospital"), be agreement in questions ("Are you ready?"), and group nouns that can take a singular or plural verb ("The audience was silent" / "The audience were silent"; "The government does not encourage" / "The government do not encourage"). Proprietary; reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Subject-Verb Agreement
sourceRecords.notes: Tier D reference. Read live via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200). The site's dedicated "a number of / the number of" lesson page is a broken link (404); the distinction is covered inside the subject-verb agreement lesson instead: "a number of" is nearly always plural because the noun after of is plural ("A number of men were strongly opposed"), while "the number of" names an arithmetical value and takes a singular verb ("The number of women was sixty-four"). Also supports none as singular or plural. Reference only; original prose.
